title: Capstone 1 kickoff: user stories and wireframes
goal: Plan a real product before coding: who it's for, what it must do, and what 'done' looks like.

concepts: The capstone: ApplyTrack, a job application tracker (Angular + Tailwind + Express + PostgreSQL + JWT)
User stories: 'As a <user>, I want <goal>, so that <reason>' with acceptance criteria
MVP vs nice-to-have: cutting scope is a skill
Low-fidelity wireframes (paper, Excalidraw, Figma)
Tracking work in GitHub Issues and a Projects board
Milestones: Week 20 backend, Week 21 frontend, Week 22 tests and deploy, Week 23 polish and portfolio

build.task: Create a NEW repo applytrack. Write docs/product.md: the problem (job seekers lose track of applications), the target user, 10–12 user stories with acceptance criteria (account, add/edit/delete applications, statuses Wishlist → Applied → Interview → Offer / Rejected, interview dates, notes, contacts, filters and search, a dashboard with counts and a weekly chart, CSV export as a stretch), and an explicit 'Not in MVP' list. Draw wireframes for login, application list, application detail/form and dashboard (desktop and mobile) and commit them as images in docs/wireframes/. Create a GitHub issue per story, with labels and milestones, on a Projects board.

hints: Good acceptance criteria are testable: 'Given I'm logged in, when I change an application's status to Interview, then it moves to the Interview column and the dashboard count updates.'
Keep the MVP small enough to finish in 2 weeks. CSV export, email reminders and file uploads are good 'later' items.
Wireframes are boxes and labels, not designs. Spend 20 minutes per screen at most.
proof: Link to the applytrack repo and its Projects board.

explainBack.q: Pick one user story and explain how you'd know it's done.
What did you leave out of the MVP and why?

lastHintExplanation: Recruiters and interviewers love candidates who can explain why they built something and how they decided what to build. User stories keep you focused on what the user needs; acceptance criteria tell you when a story is finished; a 'Not in MVP' list protects your deadline.

title: Data model: ER diagram and schema
goal: Design ApplyTrack's database properly before writing any API code.

concepts: Entities and relationships: users, applications, interviews, contacts, status history
ER diagrams with crow's foot notation (dbdiagram.io or Mermaid)
Normalisation basics: don't repeat data; one fact in one place
Enums as CHECK constraints or Postgres ENUM types
Indexes for your real queries (user_id + status, user_id + applied_on)
Audit-style history: application_status_history rows on every status change

build.task: In applytrack: draw an ER diagram (Mermaid in docs/data-model.md so it renders on GitHub) for users, applications (company, role, job_url, location, salary_range, status, source, applied_on, notes), interviews (application_id, scheduled_at, kind, outcome), contacts (application_id, name, email, role) and application_status_history (application_id, from_status, to_status, changed_at). Write the migrations with constraints and indexes, and seed.sql with a demo user and 25 realistic applications across all statuses. Under the diagram, explain each relationship, delete behaviour and index.
acceptance: Mermaid ER diagram renders on GitHub with all 5 tables
Migrations create all tables with FKs, CHECKs and NOT NULLs
Indexes match the planned list/filter/dashboard queries
Seed data covers every status and has realistic dates
docs/data-model.md explains relationships, ON DELETE choices and indexes

hints: Mermaid: erDiagram\n  USERS ||--o{ APPLICATIONS : owns\n  APPLICATIONS ||--o{ INTERVIEWS : has
Store status history from the start: the dashboard's 'applications per week' and 'time to first interview' come from it later.
applied_on is a date (a calendar day); scheduled_at is a timestamptz (a moment in time).
proof: Commit with docs/data-model.md, migrations and seed.

explainBack.q: Why store status history in a separate table instead of only the current status?
Justify one index you added with the query it speeds up.

lastHintExplanation: Only storing the current status throws away history: you can't show a timeline, count applications that reached interview, or measure how long responses take. A history table records each change as a row. Indexes should match real queries; for example, (user_id, status) supports 'my applications with status X', which the list page runs constantly.

predict.q: A user is deleted. applications.user_id has ON DELETE CASCADE, and interviews.application_id also has CASCADE. What happens to that user's interviews?

dsa.note: Each land cell starts a DFS that sinks its island; count how many times you start.

title: Backend setup: project structure and CI-ready tooling
goal: Set up the ApplyTrack API properly from the start: structure, config, lint, format and tests.

concepts: Monorepo layout: api/ and web/ in one repo
Reusing your api-starter patterns (config, errors, validate, logger)
ESLint + Prettier for consistent code
Husky + lint-staged: checks before each commit
Conventional commits (feat:, fix:, test:, docs:)

build.task: In applytrack/api: set up TypeScript (strict), Express 5, zod config validation (PORT, DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, CORS_ORIGINS, LOG_LEVEL), pino logging, the error classes and error middleware, the validate middleware, requestId, helmet, CORS, health and ready routes, the migrate script and graceful shutdown, copying the patterns (not the files blindly) from api-starter. Add ESLint, Prettier and a pre-commit hook. Scripts: dev, build, start, migrate, seed, lint, format, test. Write api/README.md with setup steps.
acceptance: npm run dev starts the API; /health and /ready work
Invalid config fails fast with clear errors
Lint and format run on commit
Migrations and seed run from npm scripts
Commits follow conventional commit style
api/README.md lets someone run it from scratch

hints: Copy deliberately: retype each file and improve it as you go. This is also a revision exercise.
npx husky init, then put npx lint-staged in .husky/pre-commit, with lint-staged running eslint --fix and prettier --write on staged .ts files.
Keep one config.ts that every module imports; never read process.env anywhere else.
proof: Link to the commit with the API foundation.

explainBack.q: Why set up lint, format and pre-commit hooks at the start of a project?
Explain your folder structure and where a new feature would go.

lastHintExplanation: Tooling is cheapest on day one: adding a linter to 5,000 lines produces hundreds of warnings, but on an empty project it keeps everything clean from the start. Pre-commit hooks stop broken or unformatted code from ever reaching the repo, which reviewers notice.

title: Auth API for ApplyTrack
goal: Implement secure registration, login and the current-user endpoint, tested from the start.

concepts: Reusing the Phase 4 auth flow: bcrypt, JWT, requireAuth
Profile update (name) and password change (requires the current password)
Rate limiting auth routes
Writing tests alongside the code

resources.title: OWASP: Forgot Password Cheat Sheet (for later)

build.task: In applytrack/api: POST /api/auth/register, POST /api/auth/login, GET /api/auth/me, PATCH /api/auth/me (name only) and POST /api/auth/change-password (requires currentPassword; new password must differ and meet the rules). Rate-limit the auth routes. Write supertest tests for every route, including the failure cases (weak password, duplicate email, wrong password, no token, expired token using a short JWT_EXPIRES_IN in tests, wrong current password). Close the matching GitHub issues from your commits ('Closes #3').
acceptance: All 5 auth routes work with correct status codes
Password change requires the current password and rejects reuse
Every route has success and failure tests (15+ tests)
No hashes in responses or logs
GitHub issues closed from commit messages

hints: Expired token test: sign a token with expiresIn: -10 (already expired) using the test secret and expect 401.
Change password: load the hash, bcrypt.compare(currentPassword), and if the new password matches the old one (bcrypt.compare(newPassword, hash)), return 400.
proof: Link to the auth commits and the closed issues.

explainBack.q: Why must change-password require the current password even though the user is logged in?
lookFor: a stolen token or unattended device shouldn't allow takeover

explainBack.q: How did you test token expiry without waiting an hour?
lookFor: or short expiry in test config

lastHintExplanation: Sensitive actions need re-authentication: if someone steals a token or uses an unlocked laptop, they still can't lock the real owner out by changing the password. Signing a token with a negative expiry produces one that's already expired, so the test is instant and deterministic.

predict.q: jwt.sign({ sub: 1 }, secret, { expiresIn: -10 }) is then verified. Result?
predict.why: Its exp is already in the past.

title: Applications API: CRUD, status changes and stats
goal: Build the core of ApplyTrack: applications with filters, status history and dashboard stats.

concepts: Changing status inside a transaction: update the application + insert history
Nested resources: /applications/:id/interviews and /contacts
Search and filters: status, company (ILIKE), applied between dates, sort, pagination
Stats endpoints with GROUP BY and date_trunc('week', ...)
Keeping controllers thin

build.task: In applytrack/api: applications CRUD scoped by user; list with status (multiple allowed), q (company or role), appliedFrom/appliedTo, sort (whitelist) and pagination. PATCH /api/applications/:id/status changes status and writes a history row in one transaction, returning 409 if the status is unchanged. GET /api/applications/:id/history. Nested CRUD for interviews and contacts. GET /api/stats returns counts per status, applications per week for the last 8 weeks (filling empty weeks with 0), and response rate (share of applied that reached interview or later).
acceptance: All application, interview and contact endpoints work, scoped by user
Status changes are transactional and recorded in history
List filters combine correctly; sort is whitelisted
Stats: per-status counts, 8-week series with zeros, response rate
Every query is parameterised

hints: Multiple statuses: ?status=Applied&status=Interview. Coerce to an array with z.union([z.string(), z.array(z.string())]).transform(v => [v].flat()), then use WHERE status = ANY($2).
Weeks with zero applications: generate the weeks with generate_series(date_trunc('week', now()) - interval '7 weeks', date_trunc('week', now()), interval '1 week') and LEFT JOIN the counts onto it.
Response rate: count applications whose history ever reached Interview, Offer or Rejected-after-interview, divided by those that reached Applied. Keep the definition simple and document it.
proof: Commit with the applications, interviews, contacts and stats features.

explainBack.q: Why must the status update and the history insert happen in one transaction?
lookFor: no history without status change or vice versa

explainBack.q: How did you make weeks with zero applications appear in the stats?

lastHintExplanation: If the status update succeeded and the history insert failed, the timeline would silently disagree with reality. A transaction makes the pair all-or-nothing. GROUP BY only returns weeks that have rows, so you generate every week with generate_series and LEFT JOIN the counts onto it, using COALESCE(count, 0) for empty weeks.

predict.q: SELECT date_trunc('week', DATE '2026-11-11') (a Wednesday). What does it return?

dsa.note: Course prerequisites form a directed graph; you can finish if there's no cycle. Use Kahn's algorithm (in-degrees + queue).

title: API test suite and week review
goal: Lock the ApplyTrack API down with a solid test suite before building the frontend on it.

concepts: Unit tests for services, API tests with supertest, DB tests for repos
Test data builders (makeApplication({ status: 'Interview' }))
Testing transactions and stats against the real test database
A coverage target as a guide, not a goal

resources.title: Kent C. Dodds: Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.

build.task: In applytrack/api: write test-data builders and an auth helper; add API tests for every applications, interviews, contacts and stats endpoint (success, validation failure, 401, IDOR 404); DB tests for the status-change transaction (forced failure leaves no partial data) and the 8-week stats query with zero weeks. Reach 80%+ line coverage on services and repos. Add a test section to api/README.md. Write week20-notes.md: what's done, what slipped, and what's next week.
acceptance: 40+ tests across unit, API and DB levels, all passing
IDOR tests for applications, interviews and contacts
Transaction and stats queries tested against real Postgres
80%+ line coverage on services and repos
week20-notes.md is honest about progress

hints: Builder: function makeApplication(overrides: Partial<NewApplication> = {}): NewApplication { return { company: 'Acme', role: 'Frontend Developer', status: 'Applied', appliedOn: '2026-11-02', ...overrides }; }
For stats tests, use vi.setSystemTime (or pass 'today' into the query) so 'the last 8 weeks' is predictable.
If a test is hard to write, the code is often too coupled. Note it and refactor the code, not just the test.
proof: Commit with the test suite and the coverage summary in the README.

explainBack.q: Which test gives you the most confidence, and why?
How do builders make tests easier to read?
lookFor: only specify what matters for the test

lastHintExplanation: Builders give every field a sensible default, so each test only states what matters to it, e.g. makeApplication({ status: 'Offer' }). The most valuable tests guard the costly failures: users seeing each other's data, half-written transactions and wrong dashboard numbers.
